analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans to cover mammograms, Pap tests, colon and prostate cancer screening.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, received no hearing, no vote, and no further action, and died when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group health plans, health insurers, and individual-market coverage to pay for routine cancer screening: yearly mammograms for women 40 and older (and high-risk younger women), clinical breast exams, annual Pap tests and pelvic exams, colon cancer screening for people 50 and older, and prostate screening for men 50 and older or at high risk, including Black men and those with a family history. It would have barred insurers from denying enrollment just to dodge the requirement, from paying people to accept weaker coverage, or from penalizing doctors who follow the rules. It would also have required plans to disclose in writing what screening benefits they cover, what patients pay out of pocket, and how to get referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer or individual health insurance who would get screening covered as a standard benefit — women needing mammograms and Pap tests, adults 50 and older needing colon and prostate screening, and high-risk people of any age, including those with a family history of cancer. The bill let the Health and Human Services Secretary update the required tests as new science emerged, at the initiative of any individual or organization that petitions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured adults due for cancer screening

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to cover annual mammograms for women 40 and older and for younger women at high risk, plus clinical breast exams on a set schedule for women 20 and older.

Requires coverage of annual Pap tests and pelvic exams for women 18 and older, colorectal cancer screening for adults 50 and older (or younger at high risk), and prostate screening for men 50 and older or at high risk, including African American men and men with a family history.

Bars insurers from denying or refusing to renew someone's coverage solely to avoid the screening requirements, from offering payments to get individuals to accept less protection, and from penalizing or rewarding providers based on whether they deliver the required care.

Requires plans to disclose annually, in writing, what screening benefits are covered, deductibles and copays, out-of-network options, and how to get referrals — so patients know what they are entitled to before they get sick.

Applies the same coverage rules to individual-market insurance, not just employer plans, and lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services update the required screening tests as medical evidence advances, including on petition from individuals or organizations.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group plans would bear the added cost of covering more screening tests, and much of that cost would likely show up in premiums shared by employers and enrollees. Public-employee plans under the federal benefits chapter would also have to comply.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not make screening free: it explicitly allows plans to keep charging deductibles, coinsurance, and copays for these services, as long as the cost-sharing does not discriminate against the covered screening benefits — so a patient's out-of-pocket cost could still be a barrier.

A mandated benefit raises costs for insurers and employers, and honest supporters would acknowledge that some of that cost passes through to premiums for everyone in a plan, including people who never use the screening.

It is a one-size-federal-mandate approach: the bill overrides what each plan and state currently covers, rather than letting states or plans tailor screening benefits, and it fixes screening intervals in statute rather than leaving them entirely to clinical judgment (though it lets a provider determine the method and frequency of colon and prostate screening).

The bill also imposes detailed disclosure paperwork on plans — annual printed statements of benefits, provider directories, and referral procedures — an administrative cost that would be borne by plan administrators and reflected in premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and direct: earlier detection of breast, cervical, colon, and prostate cancer saves lives and catches disease when treatment is cheaper and less brutal. The main costs are higher premiums and administrative paperwork, and the bill's allowance for continued cost-sharing means screening would not have been free. On balance it is a standard, well-constructed insurance mandate of the kind many states already adopted — the main criticism is not that it is badly designed, but that it never got the chance to be examined at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced, and nothing ever happened after that — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the Cancer Screening Coverage Act of 2001 in the Senate on May 10, 2001.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
One Senate Democrat signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers who sponsor plans are better off, because they never had to add the mandated screening coverage or disclosure obligations; nobody gained the coverage the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and plan sponsors never had to comply

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: The Senate committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 107th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote on the bill, so the record shows only that its sponsor and sole cosponsor were Democrats; no opposition ever went on the record.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers to pay for a defined set of cancer screening tests in both group and individual plans and to disclose benefit details in writing, adding to their claims costs. Insurers could have passed much of the added cost into premiums, but the mandate would have taken away their discretion over whether to cover these tests.

Employer plans, including plans under collective bargaining agreements (which got a delayed compliance date), would have had to add the screening benefits and disclosures, raising plan costs borne partly by employers and partly by workers' premiums.

industries.industry: Screening providers (mammography facilities, laboratories, and physicians)
industries.note: Mandatory coverage means more patients can get mammograms, Pap tests, colonoscopies, and prostate tests paid for by insurance, which means more billable services for radiology facilities, labs, and clinicians. The bill also protected providers from reimbursement cuts for complying.
